report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is partly supported, but overstated. CLA supplements may produce a **small average reduction in body fat and waist-related measures**, but evidence does not establish a reliable, clinically meaningful reduction in *abdominal/visceral* fat for most people.

A 2023 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of randomized trials concluded that CLA produced *small but statistically significant* improvements in body-composition and anthropometric outcomes, including waist circumference. This is higher-level evidence than individual trials, but “small” matters: it is not evidence of a substantial belly-fat treatment.  
https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366

The direct abdominal-fat trial often cited was a short-term randomized study in obese middle-aged men with metabolic-syndrome features—not a broad population—so its positive result cannot be generalized to everyone taking CLA.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11477497/

Earlier evidence was less encouraging: a review of 13 short-term randomized controlled human trials found little evidence that CLA reduced body weight or beneficially repartitioned fat versus lean mass.  
https://www.jlr.org/article/S0022-2275(20)31940-4/fulltext

**Bottom line:** CLA is not an evidence-based way to target abdominal fat. At best, its expected effect is modest and variable, and it should not substitute for dietary, activity, sleep, and medical approaches with much stronger evidence. Safety also deserves caution: systematic-review evidence has identified adverse changes in lipoprotein(a), a cardiovascular-risk marker, in overweight/obese participants.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8012289/
